task: Write one sentence of your own using the word reprobate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know reprobate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Family reunions still retell Great-Uncle Amos, the reprobate of the clan, who sold his cousins shares in a gold mine that never existed and toasted their health with the proceeds.
Shady is much milder than reprobate — suspicion's word, corners probably cut and questions dodged, nothing proved yet — while reprobate is a finished verdict on the whole character.
Corrupt goes further than shady — the principles are genuinely for sale — but it stops short of reprobate, which finds no principles left to sell and no shame about the vacancy.

Villainous is storybook wickedness, often theatrical — capes, schemes, a laugh pitched to reach the cheap seats. Reprobate is the sober, real-world verdict: settled, shameless wrongdoing worn in plain daylight, with no performance required and no audience needed.

Amoral means without any moral sense at all — colder and more clinical than wicked, a blank where the conscience should be, with no notion of right to defy. A reprobate knows exactly what decency demands and tramples it anyway, without a flicker of shame.

The reprobate sea captain of the old court record makes chilling reading: he sold his own crew's rations to a passing trader mid-voyage, blamed the shortage on rats, and docked the cook's pay for the missing stores.
Asked at the inquiry whether anything weighed on him, he is recorded as answering, cheerfully, 'No.'
Reprobate is the exact word for that captain, because it means morally unprincipled, wicked — and it judges the whole character, not one act.
Dishonest could describe a single lie and leave the rest of the man intact; reprobate says the rot goes all the way through, worn without shame.

It works as an adjective — a reprobate paymaster — and at least as often as a noun: an old reprobate.

Every town keeps one cautionary tale; ours was Silas Crane, who ran the only ferry across the gorge for forty years.
He overcharged widows, pocketed the toll money meant for the bridge fund, and sold 'lifetime passes' that he canceled whenever it suited him.
Called before the county board, he recited his own figures with something close to pride and paid the small fines like a man buying a license.
The word the county historian finally chose was reprobate: not merely suspected of wrong, and never pretending otherwise -- a man who knew what fairness asked and declined it daily, without shame.
When the bridge finally opened, toll-free, the town celebrated for two days.
